title: Smallest Unit Multiplier
context: Grade 5, the pages on multiplying and dividing measures. An adult sees a measure times a number. What the pages are doing is keeping every step in whole numbers by working in the smallest unit, and saying what is left over when a sharing is not even.

writeup.why: Multiply a measure by a number in its smallest unit, in whole numbers, and write the product back in the larger unit; divide a measure in its smallest unit, and say what is left over when a sharing is not even.
writeup.look: A measure card above a strip drawn to scale, copied end to end or cut into equal pieces, with any part left over kept in view.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Smallest Unit Multiplier' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of copies laid, or the number of pieces cut. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The measure card stands at x 120, y 220, 300 by 90, in deep blue, labelled Given, as a mixed measure. The Smallest unit slot sits beside it at x 460, y 220, with a violet Unit fact under it that names the link between the two units. Once the slot is filled, the measure becomes a strip drawn to scale along y 360 from x 120. The Copy button stands at x 900, y 220 and lays the strip end to end once more with each tap; the row of copies wraps onto a second line at y 440 if it runs past x 1100. The Regroup button stands at x 900, y 300 and stacks bundles of the larger unit along y 540. To divide, cut marks are dragged from a tray at x 120, y 620 onto the strip, the pieces slide apart, and the piece being measured is amber. On the fourth phase the capacity is a column of water at x 160, y 240, 120 wide, with cups along y 620. A part left over stays at the end of the strip or the bottom of the column in rose, labelled Left over. Every answer is green, labelled Answer, with its unit. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys, a delete key, a key for each unit in use, and a Left over key that opens a second slot for what is left. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. The measure the question gives, in the unit it is given in, is deep blue, labelled Given or Measure. The measure the working reaches, and a reading on a scale, is green, labelled Answer, Reading or Same measure. The places moved across the unit chart, and the worth of one small mark on a scale, are vermilion, labelled Move or One mark. A unit fact, the unit names on the chart and the other temperature scale are violet, labelled Unit fact, Unit or Other scale. The part taken away, and a part left over after sharing, are rose, labelled Taken away or Left over. The unit, column, mark or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open inside a number, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. Rulers, tapes, jugs, scales, thermometer tubes, chart lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last strip stays on the stage, copied or cut, with its answer in green and anything left over in rose.

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, when the cups fill level, the small rose part left over gives a tiny wobble at the bottom of the column, as if it is waiting to be named.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet copied or cut. On the first phase a length in metres and centimetres sits on its card with the Smallest unit slot empty. On the second a total in grams sits under its copies with the Regroup button beside it. On the third a length is drawn as one strip with the cut marks in a tray. On the fourth a capacity is drawn as a column of water with empty cups waiting beside it. One thing moves, once: the Smallest unit slot, the Regroup button, or the tray of cut marks gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.

source_tool.description: A measure card in deep blue, labelled Given, sits at the top of the working area as a mixed measure. The first job on every phase is the Smallest unit slot, where the child types the measure in its smallest unit, with a violet unit fact beside it, such as 1 m = 100 cm. The measure then becomes a strip drawn to scale. To multiply, a Copy button lays the strip end to end again, one copy a tap, and the running count at the top left of the canvas counts the copies; the total is read in the smallest unit and a Regroup button bundles it back into the larger unit, green, labelled Answer. To divide, the child drags cut marks onto the strip, the pieces slide apart, and the piece being measured is amber. When the sharing is not even, the part left over stays at the end of the strip in rose, labelled Left over, and the answer is spoken with it: so much each, with so much left over.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a unit chart of seven columns from kilo to milli with the base unit in the middle, rulers and tapes marked in their units, kitchen scales, measuring jugs marked in millilitres, and thermometers with labelled marks.
Every measure is written with its unit on every line, and every decimal names the unit it is in, so 3.04 L is never shown as a bare 3.04.
Every mixed measure shown is ordinary: its smaller part is less than one of the larger unit.
Places are counted from the unit the child has to the unit the child wants, one hop at a time, and each hop shows the number, not the unit, divided or multiplied by 10.
Multiplying and dividing a measure happen in its smallest unit, in whole numbers, and a sharing that does not come out even shows what is left over.
A thermometer shows what one small mark is worth before its column is read, and a Celsius reading sits beside a Fahrenheit one only in the four pairs the chapter prints.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a hop across the chart, a carry across units, a length shared into equal pieces, or a column rising to a mark.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a unit or a mark the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the measure the question gives is deep blue, and the measure the working reaches, with a reading taken off a scale, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The places moved across the unit chart, each one dividing or multiplying the number by 10, and the worth of one small mark on a scale are vermilion. A unit fact such as 1 kg = 1000 g, the unit names on the chart and the other temperature scale are violet. The part taken away, and a remainder left over after sharing, are rose. The unit, column, mark or step being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Move, Unit fact, Taken away, Left over and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Is the measure in its smallest unit? Start there.
voice.onNext: A new measure. Smallest unit first.
voice.opening: A measure on a card, and an empty slot for its smallest unit.
voice.onFinish: You multiplied and shared in the smallest unit, with whole numbers.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Copy or cut any strip you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has poured water from a measuring jug into four glasses of one size and seen how much was left in the jug. The tool is what copies and cuts a measure strip to scale and keeps the part left over in view.

answer_key.rule: Write the measure in its smallest unit first, so every step is in whole numbers. Multiply or divide the whole number. Then write a product back in the larger unit, with its smaller part less than one of the larger unit. When a sharing does not come out even, say how much each part gets and how much is left over, in words. Check a quotient by multiplying it back and adding what was left over.
answer_key.wrong: The stage keeps the child's working. A product regrouped wrongly stays, and beside it the bundles of the larger unit are counted out again one at a time. A quotient too big shows the last piece running past the end of the strip, in amber; a quotient too small leaves more than a piece's worth over, in amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Write the length in the smallest unit: 1 m 45 cm is 145 cm.
So 4 shelves in a row are 580 cm long.
items.question: A shelf is 1 m 45 cm long. How long are 4 shelves in a row, in centimetres?
items.checkpoint: Write the measure in its smallest unit first, so every step is in whole numbers.
items.misconception: Multiplying only the centimetres by 4 and forgetting the metres, so the shelves come out far too short.

steps: 1000 g make 1 kg, so 14,100 g is 14 kg 100 g.
As a decimal in kilograms, 14 kg 100 g is 14.1 kg.
items.question: A packet holds 2 kg 350 g of sugar. How much do 6 packets hold, in kilograms and grams?
items.checkpoint: Write the product back in the larger unit, with its smaller part less than one of the larger unit.
items.misconception: Dividing by 100 instead of by 1000 when writing the grams back in kilograms, which makes the packets ten times too heavy.

steps: Write the length in the smallest unit: 4 m 50 cm is 450 cm.
So each piece is 75 cm long.
items.question: A pipe 4 m 50 cm long is cut into 6 equal pieces. How long is each piece?
items.checkpoint: Divide in the smallest unit, in whole numbers.
items.misconception: Trying to share the 4 metres among 6 pieces and getting stuck, because the metres were not written in centimetres first.

steps: Write the capacity in the smallest unit: 1 L 850 mL is 1850 mL.
1850 divided by 4 is 462, with 2 left over.
So each cup gets 462 mL, and 2 mL is left over.
items.answer: 462 mL in each cup, with 2 mL left over in the can.
items.question: A can holds 1 L 850 mL of juice. It is shared equally among 4 cups. How much goes in each cup, and how much is left over?
items.checkpoint: When a sharing does not come out even, say how much each part gets and how much is left over, in words.
items.misconception: Leaving out the 2 mL that is left over, so the cups and the can no longer add back to the whole.

items.question: Before multiplying 3 m 5 cm by a number, write it in its smallest unit. What is it?
A string 96 cm long is cut into 4 equal pieces. How long is each piece?

A bag of 1 kg 30 g of rice is shared equally among 4 bowls. How much goes in each bowl, and how much is left over?
items.final_answer: 257 g in each bowl, with 2 g left over, because 1030 divided by 4 is 257, with 2 left over

items.question: A block of clay of 2 kg 400 g is shared equally among 8 pots. How much clay goes in each pot?

items.final_answer: 718 mL in each bottle, with 4 mL left over, because 5030 divided by 7 is 718, with 4 left over

teaching_notes: Write the measure in its smallest unit before anything is multiplied or divided, so every step is in whole numbers; the chapters so far have not taught multiplying a decimal, and it is not needed here. After multiplying, write the answer back in the larger unit. When a sharing does not come out even, say what is left over in words, and check by multiplying back and adding it. The same working finds how many packets of one size fill a vessel: both in the smallest unit, then divide.
generation_prompt: Build a measure multiplying and sharing tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A deep blue measure card sits at the top of the working area, and a Smallest unit slot takes the measure in its smallest unit, with a violet unit fact beside it. The measure becomes a strip drawn to scale. A Copy button lays the strip end to end again, a Regroup button bundles a total in the smallest unit back into the larger unit, in green, and cut marks dragged onto the strip share it into equal pieces, the piece being measured amber.
